name: Python for Absolute Beginners
description: Learn programming with Python, the most beginner-friendly language. We use real-world analogies like kitchen recipes, jars, and traffic lights to explain concepts.

lessons.title: Welcome to Python: The Friendly Snake
lessons.analogyText: Imagine a helper who follows instructions literally. If you say 'make toast,' they don't know how. You have to explain: 'Take bread, put in toaster, press lever.' Python is that assistant! Coding is just writing clear recipe-like instructions.
lessons.content: Python is a language designed to be readable. It looks a lot like normal English! It is used in web design, AI, data analysis, and automation. To show text on screen, we use the `print()` function.
lessons.codeExample:
# Tell your assistant to say hi!
print("Hello, CodeVerse!")
lessons.practiceTask: Write a line of code to print your name to the console.

lessons.title: Jars & Labels: Variables & Types
lessons.analogyText: Variables are like jars with sticky labels. If you label a jar 'cookies' and put 5 cookies inside, you can later ask for 'cookies' and get 5. If you put fresh cookies in, the old ones are replaced. In Python, `cookies = 5` creates that jar!
lessons.content: A variable is a container for storing data. Python has different types of data: String (text in quotes, like "cookies"), Integer (whole numbers, like 5), and Float (decimals, like 5.9).
lessons.codeExample:
# Label the jar 'age' and put 25 in it
age = 25

# Label another jar 'name' and put 'Alex' in it
name = "Alex"

print(name)
print(age)
lessons.practiceTask: Create a variable named `favorite_food` and assign it your favorite food as a string. Then print it.
lessons.defaultCode:
# Set favorite_food here

# Print it here

lessons.title: Talking & Listening: Input & Output
lessons.analogyText: Using `print()` is like speaking through a megaphone—the computer tells you something. Using `input()` is like holding a cup to your ear (ear trumpet)—the computer stops, waits, and listens to what you type, storing it inside a jar (variable).
lessons.content: To get information from a user, we use the `input()` function. It pauses code execution and waits for the user to type something. What they type is returned as a string.
lessons.codeExample:
print("What is your secret superpower?")
power = input()
print("Awesome! Your power is: " + power)
lessons.practiceTask: Write a program that asks the user for their favorite color and prints: 'Your color is [color]'.
lessons.practiceHint:
color = input()
print("Your color is " + color)
lessons.defaultCode:
print("What is your favorite color?")
# Read color and print the message

lessons.title: The Fork in the Road: Conditionals
lessons.analogyText: When driving, if the light is green, you GO. If it is yellow, you SLOW. Else (red), you STOP. In Python, `if`, `elif` (else if), and `else` let your code make decisions just like a driver at a traffic light.
lessons.content: We use conditional statements to perform different actions based on conditions. Conditions evaluate to True or False. We use indentation (spaces) to show which code belongs inside the decision blocks.
lessons.practiceTask: Write a program where a variable `score` is compared. If score is 50 or more, print 'Pass', else print 'Fail'.
lessons.defaultCode:
score = 75
# Check score and print Pass or Fail

lessons.title: The Hamster Wheel: Loops
lessons.analogyText: You don't brush a single tooth once and stop. You brush a tooth, check if your teeth are clean, and repeat. You do this in a loop until you are done. In Python, loops repeat code while a condition is true, or for a set list of items.
lessons.content: Python has two main loops: `for` loops (best for repeating over a list or range) and `while` loops (best for repeating until a condition changes).
lessons.codeExample:
# Loop over a range (repeats 3 times: 0, 1, 2)
for index in range(3):
    print("Brushing tooth number:", index)

# While loop
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print("Countdown:", count)
    count = count - 1
lessons.practiceTask: Write a loop that prints the phrase 'Repeat' 5 times.
lessons.practiceHint: Use: for i in range(5): print("Repeat")

lessons.title: The Recipe Book: Functions
lessons.analogyText: Instead of writing down the recipe for baking a chocolate cake every time a customer orders it, you save it in a recipe book. Now, whenever an order comes in, you simply call the 'Bake Cake' recipe! In Python, `def` defines a recipe, and calling it executes it.
lessons.content: Functions are reusable blocks of code that run when called. They can take inputs (parameters) and return outputs (results). They keep code organized and prevent copy-pasting.
lessons.codeExample:
# Define our cake-baking recipe
def bake_cake(flavor):
    return "A delicious " + flavor + " cake is ready!"

# Call our recipe
result = bake_cake("chocolate")
print(result)
lessons.practiceTask: Define a function named `greet` that takes a parameter `user_name` and returns 'Hello ' + user_name. Call it with 'Veda' and print the output.

lessons.title: Labels & Values: Dictionaries
lessons.analogyText: A contact list on your phone connects a name (Key) to a phone number (Value). You lookup 'Mom' to get her number. You don't scroll through list item #27; you lookup the key directly. A Python dictionary does exactly this!
lessons.content: Dictionaries store key-value pairs. They are written inside curly braces `{}` and values are accessed by putting their key inside square brackets `[]`.
lessons.codeExample:
contacts = {
    "Mom": "555-0199",
    "Dad": "555-0123"
}

# Lookup contact
print(contacts["Mom"])

# Add new contact
contacts["Alex"] = "555-9876"
print(contacts)
lessons.practiceTask: Create a dictionary named `inventory` with key 'apples' valued at 10. Change the value of 'apples' to 15, and print it.
lessons.defaultCode: # Create dictionary, modify apples, and print inventory['apples']

lessons.title: Project: Password Generator & Game
lessons.analogyText: Up until now, you've been learning how to use hammers, nails, and glue. Now, you're going to combine them all to build a toy chest! Building a mini project puts everything you've learned together in a real working application.
lessons.content: Let's review the Calculator code. It uses input, loops, conversions, and functions. Look at the code, play with it in the terminal, and tweak it!
lessons.practiceTask: Modify the code playground to return the sum of 50 and 15 using variables.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct variable declaration in Python?
questions.explanation: Python is dynamically typed, meaning you do not need to specify the variable type. You just write the name and assign the value!

questions.question:
What will be the output of the following code snippet?

```python
x = 10
if x > 5:
    print('Apple')
else:
    print('Orange')
```
questions.explanation: Since 10 is greater than 5, the condition x > 5 is True, and the code inside the 'if' block executes, printing 'Apple'.

questions.question:
Identify and fix the bug in this function that is supposed to double a number:

```python
def double_it(num)
    return num * 2
```
questions.explanation: In Python, defining a function requires a colon ':' at the end of the header statement (e.g., `def double_it(num):`).

name: C Programming: The Engine
description: Learn C, the language that powers operating systems and game engines. Understand compiler basics, variables, loops, arrays, and memory pointers.

lessons.title: Welcome to C: Engine Room
lessons.analogyText: Python is like telling a butler: 'Make a sandwich.' The butler handles the details. C is like designing the kitchen robot itself: you tell it which gear to spin, how much force to apply, and how much power to consume. C is closer to the hardware!
lessons.content: C is a compiled language, meaning a compiler translates your code into computer binary instructions before running. Every C program starts execution from the `main()` function.
lessons.practiceTask: Write a main function that prints: 'C is fast!'

lessons.title: Locking Types: Declaring Variables
lessons.analogyText: In Python, a jar can hold cookies today and tea tomorrow. In C, jars are rigid sorting cabinets. If you build an 'Integer cabinet,' it can ONLY hold integers. Try to put a word in it, and the robot constructor (compiler) will sound an alarm and halt build!
lessons.content: In C, you must specify the exact data type of a variable when declaring it. Common types include: `int` (whole numbers), `float` (decimals), and `char` (a single letter/symbol).
lessons.practiceTask: Declare an integer variable named `score` and assign it the value 99. Then print it using `%d`.

lessons.title: Loops in Machine Speed
lessons.analogyText: A factory loop moves box after box. In C, loops execute incredibly fast because they compile straight to machine operations. The compiler translates your `for(int i=0; i<100; i++)` into simple index-register increments.
lessons.content: C loops use similar logic to other languages: `for`, `while`, and `do-while` loops are standard. Variables must be declared before or inside the loop initialization.
lessons.practiceTask: Write a C loop that counts from 1 to 5, printing each number.
lessons.practiceHint: for(int i=1; i<=5; i++) { printf("%d", i); }

lessons.title: Street Addresses: Pointers
lessons.analogyTitle: House Addresses vs The House itself
lessons.analogyText: If you have a treasure chest, you can carry it around (heavy!). Or, you can write down its street address: '742 Evergreen Terrace.' Passing the address is fast and lets someone open the chest directly. In C, a Pointer `*p` stores the memory address of a variable.
lessons.content: Pointers are variables that store the memory address of another variable. We use the address-of operator `&` to find where a variable lives, and the dereference operator `*` to look inside the address.
lessons.practiceTask: Create an integer variable `val = 42`, a pointer `ptr` pointing to it, and print the value pointed to by `ptr` using `*ptr`.

questions.question: Which header file is required to use the standard printf() and scanf() functions in C?
questions.explanation: <stdio.h> stands for 'Standard Input/Output Header' and contains declarations for standard I/O methods like printf.
Because pointer p stores the address of a, modifying *p (the value at address p) changes the actual variable a to 20.

name: C++: The Lego Builder
description: Master C++ and Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). Learn classes, objects, inheritance, and how to build structured templates.

lessons.title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
lessons.analogyTitle: The Blueprint and the Lego Car
lessons.analogyText: A class is like an architectural blueprint. It defines: 'This object has wheels, doors, and a color.' It is not a real car yet. An object is the actual physical car built using that blueprint. You can build 5 different cars (objects) from one blueprint (class)!
lessons.content: C++ extends C by adding Object-Oriented Programming support. A Class wraps variables (attributes) and functions (methods) into a single blueprint.
lessons.practiceTask: Create a class `Dog` with a public method `bark` that prints 'Woof!'. Instantiate it in `main` and call `bark`.
lessons.practiceHint:
class Dog { public: void bark() { cout << "Woof!"; } };
int main() { Dog d; d.bark(); }

lessons.title: Inheritance: Passing the Traits
lessons.analogyText: Imagine a general blueprint for a 'Vehicle' (has speed, brand, and a start method). Instead of rewriting those traits for a 'Truck' and a 'Bicycle', the Truck simply 'inherits' them from Vehicle and adds its own custom trait: 'cargoCapacity'. C++ inheritance does exactly this!
lessons.content: Inheritance allows a child class to inherit attributes and methods of a parent class. It reduces code duplication.
lessons.practiceTask: Define a base class `Animal` with method `eat` printing 'Eating'. Create child `Cat` inheriting from `Animal`. Create Cat object in main and call `eat`.
lessons.practiceHint: class Animal { public: void eat() { cout<<"Eating"; } }; class Cat: public Animal {}; Cat c; c.eat();

questions.question: What is a Class in C++?
options: A template or blueprint for creating objects
questions.answer: A template or blueprint for creating objects
questions.explanation: A Class is a user-defined data type that serves as the blueprint for objects, wrapping members and methods together.

name: JavaScript: The Director
description: Learn JavaScript, the programming language that makes websites alive and interactive. Control button clicks, update texts on the fly, and fetch online info.

lessons.title: Welcome to JS: The Web Page Director
lessons.analogyText: HTML builds the theatre stage (walls, chairs). CSS paints the curtains and adds colored lights. JavaScript is the stage director: it tells actors when to enter, changes the props when a user presses a button, and responds to the audience clicking in real time!
lessons.content: JavaScript is a lightweight programming language built into all web browsers. It lets you add interactive behavior to web pages.
lessons.practiceTask: Write a line of code to log the sum of 10 and 20 using `console.log()`.

lessons.title: Listening for Clicks
lessons.analogyText: Imagine placing a tripwire at the door. You sit in your chair reading a book. You don't do anything until someone trips the wire, triggering the alarm bells! An 'Event Listener' is that tripwire, waiting for the user to click a button to run your function.
lessons.content: JavaScript interactive apps are built on events (clicks, keypresses, mouse movements). We use event handlers to execute code when events occur.
lessons.practiceTask: Log the text 'Click detected' to the console.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to embed JavaScript inside a web page?
questions.explanation: The standard `<script>` tag is used to enclose or link JavaScript code in an HTML file.
